aion-time.line: Passages on the aeon, enantiodromia, the quality of the moment, kairos and chronos, the world clock and the eternal return, with two statements of Van Eenwyk's.

sections.title: The aeon
sections.line: Aion (CW9ii, 1951), its foreword and ¶136, and Flying Saucers (CW10 ¶589, 1958): the Pisces aeon, and the spring-point's entry into Aquarius.

quotes.text: the Pisces aeon is the synchronistic concomitant of two thousand years of Christian development.

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

quotes.text: filled with intimations of a kind of enantiodromian reversal of dominants. I mean by this the dilemma of Christ and Antichrist

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

quotes.text: spring-point will have moved from its present position 18 degrees into Aquarius, the next aeon, that of the Water Carrier.

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

quotes.text: We are now nearing that great change which may be expected when the spring-point enters Aquarius

cite.workTitle: Civilization in Transition

sections.title: Enantiodromia
sections.line: CW6 ¶708–709, where Jung defines the term (Psychological Types, Definitions); CW13 ¶294, CW7 ¶111 and CW11 ¶526, where he uses it.

quotes.text: it is used to designate the play of opposites in the course of events—the view that everything that exists turns into its opposite.

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

quotes.text: I use the term enantiodromia for the emergence of the unconscious opposite in the course of time

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

quotes.text: every psychic development, whether individual or collective, possesses an optimum which, when exceeded, produces an enantiodromia, that is, turns into its opposite

cite.workTitle: Alchemical Studies

quotes.text: discovered the most marvellous of all psychological laws: the regulative function of opposites

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

quotes.text: What we observe here is a fundamental law of life—enantiodromia or conversion into the opposite; and it is this that makes possible the reunion of the warring halves of the personality and thereby brings the civil war to an end.

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

sections.title: The quality of the moment
sections.line: Jung on time: the quality of a moment (CW15 ¶82, Richard Wilhelm: In Memoriam, 1930), kairos (CW10 ¶398), time and energy (the seminars of 4 December 1929 and 8 June 1932) and the unconscious's space-time continuum (CW9ii ¶45).

quotes.text: whatever is born or done at this particular moment of time has the quality of this moment of time

cite.workTitle: The Spirit in Man, Art and Literature

quotes.text: it is rather the fault of kairos— the present moment in time—whose name on closer investigation turns out to be Wotan.

cite.workTitle: Civilization in Transition

quotes.text: Time is the essential identity with creative energy. There is a Greek aphorism, "Wherever there is creation, there is time." Chronos was the god of light, creation, and time.

cite.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

quotes.text: Fate evolves with time, and it is identical with time.

cite.workTitle: Visions: Notes of the Seminar 1930-1934

quotes.text: Fate and time are absolutely identical, fate being the more human aspect and time the more energic aspect. And time is another aspect of energy, for without time there is no energy, and without energy there is no time. Time is measured energy

cite.workTitle: Visions: Notes of the Seminar 1930-1934

quotes.text: finds itself in the psychically relative space-time continuum that is characteristic of the unconscious as such

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

sections.title: The world clock
sections.line: CW12 ¶307 (Psychology and Alchemy, Part II, the Vision of the World Clock) and the Zarathustra seminar's statement on the eternal return (pdf p1375).

quotes.text: There is a vertical and a horizontal circle, having a common centre. This is the world clock

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Alchemy

quotes.text: It is a circle, the eternal return. That is probably the historical origin of the idea of the apokatastasis, but that life is a circle is psychologically an archetypal idea

cite.workTitle: Nietzsche's Zarathustra: Notes of the Seminar 1934-1939

sections.title: The turn as a system
sections.line: Van Eenwyk, Archetypes and Strange Attractors (1997): two sentences from his account of chaos and order; the words are his, not Jung's.

quotes.text: designates not only where a dynamic becomes unstable, but where it becomes stable as well

cite.workTitle: Archetypes & Strange Attractors

quotes.text: order is never pure. Like the yin and the yang, it carries within it the potential to turn into its opposite. The same is true for chaos

cite.workTitle: Archetypes & Strange Attractors

archetype-as-such.line: Where Jung defines the archetype as such and sets it beside the word's ancestry, the instincts and typical situations: CW9i, CW8, CW16 and the Dream Analysis seminar of 1930.

sections.title: The model
sections.line: CW9i ¶6 and ¶155, and the Dream Analysis seminar of 12 March 1930: the archetype called a hypothetical and irrepresentable model, empty and purely formal, perfectly indescribable.

quotes.text: The archetype as such is a hypothetical and irrepresentable model

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

quotes.text: The archetype in itself is empty and purely formal

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

quotes.text: Any archetype is really perfectly indescribable, something perfectly empty, but capable of assimilating a certain kind of material of tremendous variation.

cite.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

sections.title: The name
sections.line: CW8 ¶275, in Instinct and the Unconscious (1919): Jung names Augustine as the source of the idea of the archetype; the vault records ¶270 of that essay as his first use of the term.

quotes.text: from whom I have borrowed the idea of the archetype

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: down to Malebranche and Bacon, still stands on a Platonic footing in this respect.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The instinct's side
sections.line: CW8 ¶339 (The Structure of the Psyche, 1927), CW8 ¶277 and a passage of CW16: the archetypes set beside the instincts.

quotes.text: archetypes are simply the forms which the instincts assume

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: as the self-portrait of the instinct, in exactly the same way as consciousness is an inward perception of the objective

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: an instinct is always and inevitably coupled with something like a philosophy of life

cite.workTitle: The Practice of Psychotherapy

sections.title: As many as situations
sections.line: CW9i ¶99: how many archetypes there are, in Jung's words.

quotes.text: as many archetypes as there are typical situations

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

collective-unconscious.line: Jung's statements defining the collective unconscious (CW3, CW6, CW9i), on what is inherited (CW8, CW10), on its relation to the instincts (CW8, CW9i) and on its inference from individual phenomenology (CW9ii, CW8).

sections.title: The deeper layer
sections.line: CW9i ¶2 (1934, Eranos; rev. 1954): the definition; ¶88: the collective unconscious distinguished negatively from the personal unconscious.

quotes.text: A more or less superficial layer of the unconscious is undoubtedly personal. I call it the personal unconscious. But this personal unconscious rests upon a deeper layer, which does not derive from personal experience and is not a personal acquisition but is inborn. This deeper layer I call the collective unconscious. I have chosen the term "collective" because this part of the unconscious is not individual but universal.

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

quotes.text: The collective unconscious is a part of the psyche which can be negatively distinguished from a personal unconscious by the fact that it does not, like the latter, owe its existence to personal experience

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

sections.title: The concept's birth
sections.line: CW3 ¶550 and CW6 ¶842 (Psychological Types, 1921): two earlier statements of a deeper stratum of a collective nature.

quotes.text: We must rather suppose that they are something like universally existent constituents of the unconscious psyche, which form, as it were, a deeper stratum of a collective nature

cite.workTitle: Psychogenesis of Mental Disease

quotes.text: there are other contents which do not originate in personal acquisitions but in the inherited possibility of psychic functioning in general, i.e., in the inherited structure of the brain.

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

sections.title: Inherited possibilities of ideas
sections.line: CW10 ¶14 (the 1918 form, in the vault note's dating) and CW8 ¶99: innate and inherited possibilities of ideas.

quotes.text: There are, however, innate possibilities of ideas, a priori conditions for fantasy-production, which are somewhat similar to the Kantian categories

cite.workTitle: Civilization in Transition

quotes.text: It is rather a question of inherited possibilities of ideas, “pathways” gradually traced out through the cumulative experience of our ancestors.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: Instinct and its correlates
sections.line: CW9i pdf p54 (the section The Concept of the Collective Unconscious) and CW8 ¶280, which names the instincts and their correlates, the archetypes.

quotes.text: there exists a second psychic system of a collective, universal, and impersonal nature which is identical in all individuals

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

quotes.text: The collective unconscious consists of the sum of the instincts and their correlates, the archetypes. Just as everybody possesses instincts, so he also possesses a stock of archetypal images

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: Inferred from phenomenology
sections.line: CW9ii ¶278: the existence of the collective unconscious inferred only from individual phenomenology; CW8 ¶729: a world-image that counterbalances the conscious picture of the world.

quotes.text: This disposition I have called the collective unconscious, the existence of which can be inferred only from individual phenomenology

cite.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self

quotes.text: a sort of timeless and eternal world-image which counterbalances our conscious, momentary picture of the world. It means nothing less than another world, a mirrorworld if you will

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

compensation.line: Jung's statements on compensation: the definition against Adler's use (CW6), the self-regulating psyche (CW8, CW7), dreams, neurosis, ordering factors, and one sentence of Van Eenwyk's.

sections.title: The definition
sections.line: CW6 ¶694 (Psychological Types, 1921): Jung's definition, set against Adler's restriction of the word to the balancing of inferiority feelings.

quotes.text: Whereas Adler restricts his concept of compensation to the balancing of inferiority feelings, I conceive it as functional adjustment in general, an inherent self-regulation of the psychic apparatus.

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

sections.title: The self-regulating psyche
sections.line: CW8 ¶159 and ¶132 and CW7 ¶274: the psyche called a self-regulating system like the body, and the unconscious as compensatory or complementary to the conscious.

quotes.text: Since the psyche is a self-regulating system, just as the body is, the regulating counteraction will always develop in the unconscious

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: the unconscious behaves in a compensatory or complementary manner towards the conscious

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: conscious and unconscious are not necessarily in opposition to one another, but complement one another to form a totality, which is the self

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

sections.title: The dream's other side
sections.line: CW7 ¶170 and CW18 ¶1391: Jung on dreams as compensatory to the conscious attitude.

quotes.text: in my experience the vast majority of dreams are compensatory. They always stress the other side in order to maintain the psychic equilibrium.

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

quotes.text: As a rule the meaning of a dream is compensatory to the conscious attitude, i.e., it adds to the latter what was lacking in it.

cite.workTitle: The Symbolic Life: Miscellaneous Writings

sections.title: Not opposition
sections.line: CW5 ¶98 (Symbols of Transformation) and CW16 ¶12: compensatory set beside mechanical and complementary.

quotes.text: not merely mechanical or complementary, but rather compensatory

cite.workTitle: Symbols of Transformation

quotes.text: the conscious attitude of the neurotic is unnaturally onesided and must be balanced by complementary or compensatory contents deriving from the unconscious

cite.workTitle: The Practice of Psychotherapy

sections.title: The ordering factor
sections.line: CW11 ¶447 and CW3 ¶582: the phrase compensatory ordering factor, said of a factor independent of the ego and of mandala symbols in moments of psychic disorientation.

quotes.text: a compensatory ordering factor which is independent of the ego and whose nature transcends consciousness

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

quotes.text: Mandala symbols appear very frequently in moments of psychic disorientation as compensatory ordering factors

cite.workTitle: Psychogenesis of Mental Disease

sections.title: The counteraction as a system
sections.line: Van Eenwyk, Archetypes and Strange Attractors (1997): one sentence on the shadow and compensation; the words are his, not Jung's.

quotes.text: Because the shadow compensates consciousness, whenever we think we know what the shadow is, its opposite automatically begins to emerge from the unconscious

cite.workTitle: Archetypes & Strange Attractors

complex.line: Jung's statements on the complex from the association experiments (CW2) to the restatement of 1934 (CW8), with the passages on its autonomy and on energy.

sections.title: The founding definition
sections.line: CW2 ¶166 (1904–05): the definition of the emotionally charged complex; CW18 ¶832: Jung on how the experiments led him to the word.

quotes.text: By "emotionally charged complex" we mean the sum of ideas referring to a particular feeling-toned event. We shall always use the term "complex" in this sense in what follows.

cite.workTitle: Experimental Researches

quotes.text: I found then that the experiments were almost regularly disturbed by psychic factors beyond the control of consciousness. I called them complexes

cite.workTitle: The Symbolic Life: Miscellaneous Writings

sections.title: How a complex behaves
sections.line: CW2 ¶902, ¶861 and ¶1353, and CW11 ¶21: the complex as a second personality to which ego-consciousness is subjected, and as secondary or partial personalities.

quotes.text: The complex plays the part of a second and stronger personality, to which ego-consciousness is subjected.

cite.workTitle: Experimental Researches

quotes.text: This second personality devours what is left of the normal ego and forces it into the role of a secondary (oppressed) complex

cite.workTitle: Experimental Researches

quotes.text: because the complexes behave quite independently of the ego, and force upon it a quasi-foreign will

cite.workTitle: Experimental Researches

quotes.text: Complexes do indeed behave like secondary or partial personalities possessing a mental life of their own.

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

sections.title: What one is
sections.line: CW8 ¶200–201 and ¶204 (1934, A Review of the Complex Theory): Jung's definition of the feeling-toned complex, his statement that complexes can have us, and his naming them splinter psyches.

quotes.text: What then, scientifically speaking, is a "feeling-toned complex"? It is the image of a certain psychic situation which is strongly accentuated emotionally and is, moreover, incompatible with the habitual attitude of consciousness.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Everyone knows nowadays that people "have complexes." What is not so well known, though far more important theoretically, is that complexes can have us.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Today we can take it as moderately certain that complexes are in fact "splinter psyches."

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The ground of psychic life
sections.line: CW2 ¶664 and ¶610 on complexes and the background of consciousness, and the Dream Analysis seminar (pdf p442) on complexes and energy.

quotes.text: The background of our consciousness (or the unconscious) consists of such complexes

cite.workTitle: Experimental Researches

quotes.text: directed by a psychic factor that can behave like an independent being

cite.workTitle: Experimental Researches

quotes.text: without complexes there can be no energy. They are the focus and very mother of energy

cite.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

individuation.line: Jung's definitions and statements on individuation (CW6, CW7, CW9i, CW12, CW16, CW14), with the passages that name its two aspects, its aim, and the two tensions the vault note records.

sections.title: The process
sections.line: CW6 ¶757, ¶758 and ¶762 (Definitions, 1921): the definition, and individuation as a natural necessity and as the development of consciousness out of the original state of identity.

quotes.text: In general, it is the process by which individual beings are formed and differentiated; in particular, it is the development of the psychological individual (q.v.) as a being distinct from the general, collective psychology.

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

quotes.text: Individuation is practically the same as the development of consciousness out of the original state of identity

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

quotes.text: Individuation is a natural necessity inasmuch as its prevention by a levelling down to collective standards is injurious to the vital activity of the individual.

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

sections.title: Becoming an 'in-dividual'
sections.line: CW7 ¶266 (1928), CW12 ¶330 and CW9i ¶490: Jung's statements of what the word means, as in-dividual, as self and as whole.

quotes.text: Individuation means becoming an “in-dividual,” and, in so far as “individuality” embraces our innermost, last, and incomparable uniqueness, it also implies becoming one’s own self.

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

quotes.text: In the last analysis every life is the realization of a whole, that is, of a self, for which reason this realization can also be called “individuation.”

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Alchemy

quotes.text: that is, a separate, indivisible unity or "whole."

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

sections.title: Two aspects
sections.line: CW16 ¶448: the two principal aspects Jung names; CW7 ¶269: the aim of individuation as he states it against the persona and primordial images.

quotes.text: Individuation has two principal aspects: in the first place it is an internal and subjective process of integration, and in the second it is an equally indispensable process of objective relationship

cite.workTitle: The Practice of Psychotherapy

quotes.text: The aim of individuation is nothing less than to divest the self of the false wrappings of the persona on the one hand, and of the suggestive power of primordial images on the other

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

sections.title: The aim, and what it costs
sections.line: CW7 ¶405 on the goal of individuation, CW14 ¶778 on the experience of the self and the ego, CW9i ¶256 on its psychological meaning and CW9i ¶705 on the union of opposites.

quotes.text: Sensing the self as something irrational, as an indefinable existent, to which the ego is neither opposed nor subjected, but merely attached, and about which it revolves very much as the earth revolves round the sun—thus we come to the goal of individuation.

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

quotes.text: For this reason the experience of the self is always a defeat for the ego

cite.workTitle: Mysterium Coniunctionis

quotes.text: In its psychological meaning, individuation is an opus contra naturam

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

quotes.text: but the painful experience of the union of opposites.

cite.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious

sections.title: What it requires
sections.line: CW7 ¶505: the dissolution of the persona as an indispensable condition, and what Jung says of conscious intention.

quotes.text: The dissolution of the persona is therefore an indispensable condition for individuation. It is, however, impossible to achieve individuation by conscious intention

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

libido.line: Jung's statements on libido: its definition as an energy-value (CW5), the energic viewpoint (CW4, CW5), canalization, mana and the types, and one sentence of Van Eenwyk's.

sections.title: The redefinition
sections.line: CW5 ¶197 (the 1928 revision of Wandlungen, in the vault note's dating): the definition of libido as an energy-value.

quotes.text: We would be better advised, therefore, when speaking of libido, to understand it as an energy-value which is able to communicate itself to any field of activity whatsoever, be it power, hunger, hatred, sexuality, or religion, without ever being itself a specific instinct.

cite.workTitle: Symbols of Transformation

sections.title: The energic viewpoint
sections.line: CW4 ¶567 and CW5 ¶189: psychological phenomena as manifestations of energy, and libido set beside energy in physics since Robert Mayer.

quotes.text: All psychological phenomena can be considered as manifestations of energy, in the same way that all physical phenomena have been understood as energic manifestations ever since Robert Mayer discovered the law of the conservation of energy.

cite.workTitle: Freud and Psychoanalysis

quotes.text: the concept of libido in psychology has functionally the same significance as the concept of energy in physics since the time of Robert Mayer

cite.workTitle: Symbols of Transformation

sections.title: Not one instinct
sections.line: CW5 ¶185: the reason Jung gives against a one-sided definition of libido.

quotes.text: The very fact that it is impossible to derive the whole mass of psychic phenomena from a single instinct forbids a one-sided definition of “libido.”

cite.workTitle: Symbols of Transformation

sections.title: Canalization
sections.line: CW5 ¶337, ¶344 and ¶398: the archetypes as river-beds of psychic life, symbols as transformers of libido, and sacrifice as a canalization of libido.

quotes.text: the archetypes are the forms or river-beds along which the current of psychic life has always flowed

cite.workTitle: Symbols of Transformation

quotes.text: The symbols act as transformers, their function being to convert libido from a “lower” into a “higher” form.

cite.workTitle: Symbols of Transformation

quotes.text: The sacrifice is the very reverse of regression—it is a successful canalization of libido into the symbolic equivalent of the mother, and hence a spiritualization of it

cite.workTitle: Symbols of Transformation

sections.title: The charge
sections.line: CW8 ¶128 (the primitive view of mana as a forerunner of the concept of psychic energy), CW5 ¶170 (libido as by nature daemonic) and CW6 ¶869 (the localization of libido in the types).

quotes.text: We cannot escape the impression that the primitive view of mana is a forerunner of our concept of psychic energy and, most probably, of energy in general.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: As a power which transcends consciousness the libido is by nature daemonic: it is both God and devil

cite.workTitle: Symbols of Transformation

quotes.text: The expressions, therefore, used by James show clearly that the difference between the types is the result of a different localization of the libido, this “magical power” in the depth of our being, which, depending on the individual, is directed sometimes to our inner life, sometimes to the objective world.

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

sections.title: The current as a system
sections.line: Van Eenwyk, Archetypes and Strange Attractors (1997): his phrase for what archetypes do with psychic energy; the words are his, not Jung's.

quotes.text: a kind of alternating current between consciousness and the unconscious

cite.workTitle: Archetypes & Strange Attractors

mana.line: Jung's statements on mana: Lehmann's definition and the primitive energetics around it (CW8), its occurrence in CW10 and CW16, the mana-personality (CW7) and later uses.

sections.title: The definition
sections.line: CW8 ¶114 and ¶128 (On Psychic Energy, 1928): the thesis on a magical potency, Lehmann's definition of mana, and Jung's remark that the primitive view of mana is a forerunner of the concept of psychic energy.

quotes.text: the most primitive ideas concerning a magical potency, which is regarded both as an objective force and as a subjective state of intensity.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: In his classic study of mana Lehmann defines it as something "extraordinarily effective."

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: We cannot escape the impression that the primitive view of mana is a forerunner of our concept of psychic energy and, most probably, of energy in general.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: An experience, not a concept
sections.line: CW10 ¶128 (the thing which is astonishing), CW16 ¶4 (mana as a universal medicinal or healing power) and CW8 ¶130 (the need to represent the sensed dynamism of psychic events in a concrete way).

quotes.text: In the face of something extraordinary it is not he who is astonished, but rather the thing which is astonishing.

cite.workTitle: Civilization in Transition

quotes.text: Mana is a universal medicinal or healing power which renders men, animals, and plants fruitful and endows chieftain and medicine-man with magical strength.

cite.workTitle: The Practice of Psychotherapy

quotes.text: even at early levels of human consciousness man felt the need to represent the sensed dynamism of psychic events in a concrete way

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The reservations
sections.line: CW8 ¶127: mana called a representation and not a concept; CW8 ¶129: Jung, following Lehmann, writes that nothing divine attaches to mana.

quotes.text: Thus mana is not a concept but a representation based on the perception of a "phenomenal" relationship.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: nothing "divine" attaches to mana, so that one cannot see in mana the original form of an idea of God.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The mana-personality
sections.line: CW7 ¶388: Jung's name for a personality consistent with the extraordinarily potent (Napoleon and Lao-tzu are the two figures in the passage), and what he says it corresponds to.

quotes.text: It corresponds to a dominant of the collective unconscious, to an archetype which has taken shape in the human psyche through untold ages of just that kind of experience.

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

sections.title: Mana now
sections.line: CW10 ¶845 and ¶583 (Civilization in Transition): two later uses of the word, for conscience and for the effect of deepened consciousness.

quotes.text: Conscience is a manifestation of mana, of the “extraordinarily powerful,” a quality which is the especial peculiarity of archetypal ideas.

cite.workTitle: Civilization in Transition

quotes.text: The deepening and broadening of his consciousness produce the kind of effect which the primitives call “mana.”

cite.workTitle: Civilization in Transition

numinosum.line: Jung's uses of Otto's word: its definition in CW11 ¶6, and later passages in CW8, CW10 and CW18.

sections.title: The term
sections.line: CW11 ¶6 and ¶9 (Psychology and Religion): Jung credits Rudolf Otto with the word and gives his own definition; ¶9 on religion and the experience of the numinosum.

quotes.text: On the contrary, it seizes and controls the human subject, who is always rather its victim than its creator.

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

quotes.text: The numinosum is either a quality belonging to a visible object or the influence of an invisible presence that causes a peculiar alteration of consciousness.

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

quotes.text: the attitude peculiar to a consciousness which has been changed by experience of the numinosum

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

sections.title: What it does to a person
sections.line: CW8 ¶216, where Jung again credits Otto's expression, and CW18 ¶787, where he lists what belongs to a nocturnal, numinous experience.

quotes.text: the numinosum, to use an apt expression of Rudolf Otto's

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: An integral component of any nocturnal, numinous experience is the dimming of consciousness, the feeling that one is in the grip of something greater than oneself, the impossibility of exercising criticism, and the paralysis of the will

cite.workTitle: The Symbolic Life: Miscellaneous Writings

sections.title: Never indifferent
sections.line: CW8 ¶405: Jung on the numinous character of the archetypes when they appear, and on its effects.

quotes.text: the archetypes have, when they appear, a distinctly numinous character which can only be described as "spiritual," if "magical" is too strong a word

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: It can be healing or destructive, but never indifferent, provided of course that it has attained a certain degree of clarity.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: In a life
sections.line: CW10 ¶864, ¶871 and ¶874 (Good and Evil in Analytical Psychology): the numinosum, the tremendum and the fascinosum.

quotes.text: Anything that comes upon me with this intensity I experience as numinous, no matter whether I call it divine or devilish or just “fate.”

cite.workTitle: Civilization in Transition

quotes.text: Consciousness experiences this supraordinate totality as something numinous, as a tremendum or fascinosum

cite.workTitle: Civilization in Transition

quotes.text: I am face to face with what Rudolf Otto calls the tremendum and fascinosum. I cannot "conquer" a numinosum, I can only open myself to it, let myself be overpowered by it, trusting in its meaning

cite.workTitle: Civilization in Transition

sections.title: And the doctrines
sections.line: CW18 ¶1160: the numinous quality of the archetypes, and what Jung says follows for theology.

quotes.text: As the archetypes have a “numinous” quality and underlie all religious and dogmatic ideas, depth psychology is also of importance for theology.

cite.workTitle: The Symbolic Life: Miscellaneous Writings

participation-mystique.line: Jung's definition of Lévy-Bruhl's term (CW6), his statements on what it means (CW10, CW17), its form between two people, and its occurrences in art, alchemy and the analogies of the unconscious.

sections.title: The definition
sections.line: CW6 ¶781 (Psychological Types, Definitions, 1921): Jung's definition of the term, which he attributes to Lévy-Bruhl; a footnote in CW18 (pdf p933) on Lévy-Bruhl's retraction.

quotes.text: It denotes a peculiar kind of psychological connection with objects, and consists in the fact that the subject cannot clearly distinguish himself from the object but is bound to it by a direct relationship which amounts to partial identity (q.v.).

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

quotes.text: Lévy-Bruhl later retracted this term under the pressure of adverse criticism, to which he unfortunately succumbed. His critics were wrong inasmuch as unconscious identity is a well-known psychological fact.

sections.title: Identity, not sympathy
sections.line: CW10 ¶69 and ¶130 and CW17 ¶83: Jung's statements of what the term means, and of the word mystical.

quotes.text: To put it briefly, it means a state of identity in mutual unconsciousness.

cite.workTitle: Civilization in Transition

quotes.text: There is nothing “mystical” about identity, any more than there is anything mystical about the metabolism common to mother and embryo.

quotes.text: Lévy-Bruhl has coined the expression participation mystique for these remarkable relationships. It seems to me that the word “mystical” is not happily chosen.

sections.line: CW10 ¶852: what Jung says happens when a dialogue between two people touches something fundamental, essential and numinous.

quotes.text: It is an unconscious identity in which two individual psychic spheres interpenetrate to such a degree that it is impossible to say what belongs to whom

sections.line: CW15 ¶162 on artistic creation, CW14 ¶336 on the alchemists and their substance, and CW5 ¶203, the vault note's earliest adoption of the term (Wandlungen, 1912).

quotes.text: a state of participation mystique, or unconscious identity, arose between them and the chemical substance

persona.line: Jung's statements on the persona: its definition (CW6), its description as a mask and as a compromise between individual and society (CW7), the mask worn by the collective psyche, and the dissolution of the persona.

sections.title: The mask
sections.line: CW6 ¶800 (Definitions, 1921), CW7 ¶305 and ¶246: the name from the masks of actors in antiquity, and Jung's descriptions of the persona as a kind of mask and as a compromise between individual and society.

quotes.text: This mask, i.e., the ad hoc adopted attitude, I have called the persona, which was the name for the masks worn by actors in antiquity.

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

quotes.text: a complicated system of relations between the individual consciousness and society, fittingly enough a kind of mask, designed on the one hand to make a definite impression upon others, and, on the other, to conceal the true nature of the individual

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

quotes.text: Fundamentally the persona is nothing real: it is a compromise between individual and society as to what a man should appear to be.

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

sections.title: Its function
sections.line: CW6 ¶801: Jung's definition of the persona as a functional complex concerned with the relation to objects.

quotes.text: a functional complex that comes into existence for reasons of adaptation or personal convenience, but is by no means identical with the individuality. The persona is exclusively concerned with the relation to objects

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

sections.line: CW7 ¶465 (the mask worn by the collective psyche) and CW18 ¶1334 (the persona as a composite of the individual's behaviour and the role attributed to him by the public).

quotes.text: It is, as its name implies, only the mask worn by the collective psyche, a mask that feigns individuality

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

quotes.text: The persona is never the true character; it is a composite of the individual's behaviour and of the role attributed to him by the public

quotes.text: Anyone who is himself his outward role will infallibly succumb to the inner processes

psychoid.line: Where Jung uses the word and what he says it names: in the essays of 1946–1954, in the synchronicity essay, and in his letters with the physicist Wolfgang Pauli.

sections.title: The naming
sections.line: The synchronicity essay (CW8 ¶840, 1952) says what Jung has named psychoid and why.

quotes.text: The latter represents a psyche that is identical in all individuals.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: It cannot be directly perceived or "represented," in contrast to the perceptible psychic phenomena, and on account of its "irrepresentable" nature I have called it "psychoid."

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The three reservations
sections.line: On the Nature of the Psyche (CW8 ¶368): the three reservations on his use of the word, and Bleuler as its source.

quotes.text: I do so with three reservations: firstly, I use it as an adjective, not as a noun; secondly, no psychic quality in the proper sense of the word is implied, but only a "quasi-psychic" one such as the reflex-processes possess; and thirdly, it is meant to distinguish a category of events from merely vitalistic phenomena on the one hand and from specifically psychic processes on the other.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: although it is always the function that creates its own organ, and maintains or modifies it.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: although my use of the term derives from a different field of perception, it nevertheless seeks to delineate roughly the same group of phenomena that Bleuler had in mind.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The form under the image
sections.line: The Spirit Mercurius (CW13 ¶350): the psychoid form underlying an archetypal image.

quotes.text: The psychoid form underlying any archetypal image retains its character at all stages of development, though empirically it is capable of endless variations.

cite.workTitle: Alchemical Studies

sections.title: The ultra-violet end
sections.line: On the Nature of the Psyche (CW8 ¶417): the archetype as such is placed at the ultra-violet end of the psychic spectrum.

quotes.text: The archetypal representations (images and ideas) mediated to us by the unconscious should not be confused with the archetype as such. They are very varied structures which all point back to one essentially "irrepresentable" basic form.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: The latter is characterized by certain formal elements and by certain fundamental meanings, although these can be grasped only approximately.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: The archetype as such is a psychoid factor that belongs, as it were, to the invisible, ultraviolet end of the psychic spectrum.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Since other archetypes give rise to similar doubts, it seems to me probable that the real nature of the archetype is not capable of being made conscious, that it is transcendent, on which account I call it psychoid.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The physics parallel
sections.line: CW8 ¶419–420: the psychic spectrum set beside the physicist's irrepresentable models, and what Jung says follows for psyche and matter.

quotes.text: When the existence of two or more irrepresentables is assumed, there is always the possibility—which we tend to overlook—that it may not be a question of two or more factors but of one only.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: The identity or non-identity of two irrepresentable quantities is something that cannot be proved.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Since psyche and matter are contained in one and the same world, and moreover are in continuous contact with one another and ultimately rest on irrepresentable, transcendental factors, it is not only possible but fairly probable, even, that psyche and matter are two different aspects of one and the same thing.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Just as the "psychic infra-red," the biological instinctual psyche, gradually passes over into the physiology of the organism and thus merges with its chemical and physical conditions, so the "psychic ultra-violet," the archetype, describes a field which exhibits none of the peculiarities of the physiological and yet, in the last analysis, can no longer be regarded as psychic, although it manifests itself psychically.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Although there is no form of existence that is not mediated to us psychically and only psychically, it would hardly do to say that everything is merely psychic.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: the psyche and its contents are the only reality which is given to us ioithout a medium.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The specific charge
sections.line: CW8 ¶841, the paragraph after the naming: what the archetypes are said to be and to do.

quotes.text: The archetypes are formal factors responsible for the organization of unconscious psychic processes: they are "patterns of behaviour."

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: At the same time they have a "specific charge" and develop numinous effects which express themselves as affects.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: Not localized in one person
sections.line: Flying Saucers: A Modern Myth (CW10 ¶851): how the psychoid archetype is said to behave.

quotes.text: The psychoid archetype has a tendency to behave as though it were not localized in one person but were active in the whole environment.

cite.workTitle: Civilization in Transition

sections.line: Atom and Archetype, the Pauli–Jung letters: Jung's statements of 1951 and 1953 on the archetype's physical and psychic occurrence.

quotes.text: With the merely psychoid (transcendental) nature of the archetype, its purely physical occurrence is by no means precluded.

cite.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

quotes.text: it is based on the psychoid archetype, which, as experience has shown, can be express itseII both psychically and physically.

cite.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

quotes.text: The characteristic that is peculiar to the archetype is that it manifests itself not only psychically-subjectively but also physically-objectively

cite.workTitle: Atom and Archetype: The Pauli/Jung Letters

sections.line: Letter 63 (October 1953): Jung on whole numbers and the psychoid archetype.

quotes.text: that they are as much inside as outside. Thus, one can never make out whether they have been devised or discovered; as numbers they are inside and as a quantity they are outside.

sections.line: Pauli's own words: the objection of December 1950, and a letter of December 1953 (66P).

sections.line: CW8 ¶599, a note added in 1948 to 'The Psychological Foundations of Belief in Spirits'.

quotes.text: Not only the findings of parapsychology, but my own theoretical reflections, outlined in "On the Nature of the Psyche," have led me to certain postulates which touch on the realm of nuclear physics and the conception of the space-time continuum. This opens up the whole question of the transpsychic reality immediately underlying the psyche.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: The last word
sections.line: CW18 ¶1208, a letter to Michael Fordham (1955): the term in its late form.

quotes.text: Synchronicity tells us something about the nature of what I call the psychoid factor, i.e., the unconscious archetype (not its conscious representation!).

cite.workTitle: The Symbolic Life: Miscellaneous Writings

synchronicity.line: Jung's definition of synchronicity in CW8 (1952), its two factors, its description as an acausal orderedness, and two statements on where the word came from.

sections.title: The definition
sections.line: CW8 ¶849–850 (Synchronicity: An Acausal Connecting Principle, 1952): the definition, and the distinction from synchronism.

quotes.text: Synchronicity therefore means the simultaneous occurrence of a certain psychic state with one or more external events which appear as meaningful parallels to the momentary subjective state—and, in certain cases, vice versa.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: I am therefore using the general concept of synchronicity in the special sense of a coincidence in time of two or more causally unrelated events which have the same or a similar meaning, in contrast to "synchronism," which simply means the simultaneous occurrence of two events.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: A principle, in its own right
sections.line: CW8 ¶840, ¶858 and ¶965: the term as a hypothetical factor equal in rank to causality, the two factors of synchronicity, and acausal orderedness.

quotes.text: I have picked on the term "synchronicity" to designate a hypothetical factor equal in rank to causality as a principle of explanation.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: Synchronicity therefore consists of two factors: a) An unconscious image comes into consciousness either directly (i.e., literally) or indirectly (symbolized or suggested) in the form of a dream, idea, or premonition, b) An objective situation coincides with this content

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: The meaningful coincidence or equivalence of a psychic and a physical state that have no causal relationship to one another means, in general terms, that it is a modality without a cause, an "acausal orderedness."

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.title: Not a cause, an orderedness
sections.line: CW8 ¶947: synchronicity called a highly abstract and irrepresentable quantity with a psychoid property; CW8 ¶440: what Jung says happens to the synchronistic marginal phenomena once a psychic content crosses the threshold of consciousness.

quotes.text: I am only too conscious that synchronicity is a highly abstract and "irrepresentable" quantity. It ascribes to the moving body a certain psychoid property which, like space, time, and causality, forms a criterion of its behaviour.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: As soon as a psychic content crosses the threshold of consciousness, the synchronistic marginal phenomena disappear, time and space resume their accustomed sway, and consciousness is once more isolated in its subjectivity

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

sections.line: The Dream Analysis seminar (4 December 1929, pdf p443), where Jung says he has invented the word, and the editorial preface of the monograph's volume (pdf p13), which quotes Jung on Einstein's influence.

quotes.text: things happening at the same moment as an expression of the same time content

cite.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

quotes.text: it was he who first started me off thinking about a possible relativity of time as well as space, and their psychic conditionality

transcendent-function.line: Jung's definitions and statements on the transcendent function (CW6, CW7, CW8, CW11, CW14, CW18) and the Dream Analysis seminar, with one sentence of Van Eenwyk's.

sections.title: The name
sections.line: CW6 ¶184 (1921), CW8 ¶131, CW6 ¶828 and CW7 ¶121: Jung's definitions of the name and his comparison with a mathematical function; in the Dream Analysis seminar of 4 June 1930 (pdf p674) he says he did not take the term from higher mathematics.

quotes.text: This function of mediation between the opposites I have termed the transcendent function, by which I mean nothing mysterious, but merely a combined function of conscious and unconscious elements, or, as in mathematics, a common function of real and imaginary quantities.

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

quotes.text: There is nothing mysterious or metaphysical about the term "transcendent function." It means a psychological function comparable in its way to a mathematical function of the same name, which is a function of real and imaginary numbers.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: “function” being here understood not as a basic function but as a complex function made up of other functions, and “transcendent” not as denoting a metaphysical quality but merely the fact that this function facilitates a transition from one attitude to another.

cite.workTitle: Psychological Types

quotes.text: It has been named the “transcendent function” because it represents a function based on real and “imaginary,” or rational and irrational, data, thus bridging the yawning gulf between conscious and unconscious.

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

quotes.text: I did not take that term from higher mathematics, I learned only later that the same term was used there, meaning the same thing

cite.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

sections.title: The transition
sections.line: CW8 ¶145 and CW11 ¶780: why Jung says it is called transcendent, and that it is a process and a method at the same time.

quotes.text: It is called "transcendent" because it makes the transition from one attitude to another organically possible, without loss of the unconscious.

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: The whole process is called the “transcendent function.” It is a process and a method at the same time.

cite.workTitle: Psychology and Religion: West and East

sections.title: The living third
sections.line: CW8 ¶189 (a living, third thing), CW7 ¶360 (the secret of alchemy) and the Dream Analysis seminar (pdf p674) on the tortoise.

quotes.text: The confrontation of the two positions generates a tension charged with energy and creates a living, third thing

cite.workTitle: The Structure and Dynamics of the Psyche

quotes.text: The secret of alchemy was in fact the transcendent function, the transformation of personality through the blending and fusion of the noble with the base components, of the differentiated with the inferior functions, of the conscious with the unconscious.

cite.workTitle: Two Essays on Analytical Psychology

quotes.text: The characteristics of the tortoise are the characteristics of the transcendent function, the one that unites the pairs of opposites

cite.workTitle: Dream Analysis: Notes of the Seminar

sections.title: The method
sections.line: CW14 ¶257 (Mysterium Coniunctionis) and CW18 ¶1554 (1954, in the vault note's dating): Jung on getting to know the counterposition in the unconscious and on the cooperation of conscious reasoning with the data of the unconscious.

quotes.text: This continual process of getting to know the counterposition in the unconscious I have called the “transcendent function,” because the confrontation of conscious (rational) data with those that are unconscious (irrational) necessarily results in a modification of standpoint.

cite.workTitle: Mysterium Coniunctionis

quotes.text: The cooperation of conscious reasoning with the data of the unconscious is called the “transcendent function”

cite.workTitle: The Symbolic Life: Miscellaneous Writings
